question: Why do nurses document patient care?

options.A: To prove the nurse worked a full shift
options.B: To provide data for hospital billing only
options.D: To communicate care among the healthcare team

explanation: Great job! Writing things down ensures doctors, nurses on other shifts, and therapists all know what is happening with your patient.

question: How can bad or missing documentation put a patient in danger?

options.A: It automatically increases the patient's hospital bill
options.B: It can lead to missed interventions and errors
options.C: It causes delays in hospital discharge procedures
options.D: It prevents doctors from writing new prescriptions

explanation: Spot on! If care details are missing, the next nurse might repeat a treatment or miss a dangerous change in the patient's condition.

question: In a court of law, how is a patient's medical record treated?

options.D: As a draft of medical opinions

explanation: That is right! Charts are legal evidence used to prove whether or not proper care was given.

question: A hospital manager checks patient charts to see if a new pain relief guide is working well. What goal does this support?
explanation: Correct! Looking back at charts helps the hospital find ways to upgrade patient care and nursing protocols.

question: What does it mean to write a 'contemporaneous' nursing note?

options.A: It is written using official medical shorthand
options.B: It is written at the end of the entire work week
options.C: It is written close to the time care is given
options.D: It is written by a senior doctor only

explanation: Spot on! Writing notes right away means you don't have to rely on memory, keeping the true timeline safe.

question: Why is the nursing rule 'if it wasn't charted, it wasn't done' so important?

options.A: Courts rely on written records as proof of care
options.B: Patients can demand a refund for missing notes
options.C: Hospitals refuse to pay nurses for unwritten tasks
options.D: Doctors will repeat every task not found in text

explanation: That is correct! Legally, if you didn't write it down, the court assumes the care never happened, no matter how hard you worked.

question: Which of these is a factual note rather than a personal opinion?

options.A: Patient refuses medication because they are difficult
options.B: Patient states pain level is 8 out of 10
options.C: Patient is acting very annoying today
options.D: Patient seems depressed about their diagnosis

explanation: Well done! Stating exact numbers and direct quotes keeps your charting objective and free from personal bias.

question: Which of these actions breaks the rule of current, truthful documentation?

options.A: Updating the care plan after assessing a new wound
options.B: Charting routine morning vital signs before taking them
options.C: Writing a note ten minutes after giving an injection
options.D: Recording a patient's reaction right after a procedure

explanation: Spot on! Charting care before you actually do it is falsification and is dangerous and illegal.

question: In SOAP charting, what kind of details go into the 'O' (Objective) section?

options.A: The patient's personal feelings and complaints
options.B: The nurse's personal opinion about the diagnosis
options.C: Measurable data like vital signs and lab results
options.D: The future medical orders written by the doctor

explanation: Correct! Objective data means facts you can measure, see, or test, like blood pressure and lab values.

question: What is the main benefit of Charting by Exception (CBE)?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any nursing signatures
options.B: It reduces redundant writing by focusing on abnormal findings
options.C: It prevents patients from reading their own medical charts
options.D: It allows nurses to skip physical head-to-toe assessments

explanation: That is right! CBE assumes everything is normal unless you write down an exception, which saves precious time on a busy shift.

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the SBAR communication tool?
explanation: Spot on! 'B' stands for Background, giving the history and context that led up to the current issue.

question: A nurse notices a patient's blood pressure just dropped suddenly and calls the doctor. What is the best way to handle this report?

options.A: Describe the patient's childhood medical history in detail
options.B: State the current vital signs and request specific orders
options.C: Ask the doctor to review the entire paper chart in person
options.D: Wait until the end of the shift to mention the blood pressure drop

explanation: Great choice! When calling a doctor, give clear, current facts right away and ask for what the patient needs now.

question: Where should a nurse document that an incident report was filled out?

options.A: In the nursing care plan under safety goals
options.B: On the front cover of the patient's bedside folder
options.C: Nowhere in the patient's clinical chart
options.D: In the progress notes under objective data

explanation: Spot on! Incident reports are internal hospital documents kept completely separate from the patient's official medical record.

question: Why do healthcare facilities use incident reports?

options.A: To calculate the patient's final hospital expenses
options.B: To improve safety and prevent future occurrences
options.C: To provide permanent legal evidence inside patient charts
options.D: To find which specific nurse to blame for a mistake

explanation: That is right! Incident reports help hospitals catch system hazards so they can fix policies and protect future patients.

question: What is the proper way to fix a writing error on a paper nursing chart?

options.A: Tear out the entire page and rewrite the nursing notes
options.B: Draw a single line through the error and write your initials
options.C: Scratch out the wrong words until they disappear
options.D: Cover the mistake completely with thick correction fluid

explanation: Well done! Drawing a single line keeps the original words readable while showing it was corrected, preventing any look of tampering.

question: Which of these charting entries is poorly written?

options.A: Wound measures 3 cm by 2 cm with no foul drainage
options.B: Patient slept quietly for four hours through the night
options.C: Patient walked 20 meters in the hallway with a walker
options.D: Patient appears to be in a very bad mood today

explanation: Correct! Vague labels like 'bad mood' are judgmental. Always write down the exact behaviors you observe instead.
